name: Network Security Toolkit
summary: A specialized Fedora-based bootable live operating system engineered for network security auditing, packet analysis, and system administration, featuring an advanced Web User Interface (WUI) managing over 250 security tools.
license: GPL-2.0-or-later and upstream open-source tool licenses

content.introduction: Network Security Toolkit (NST) is an open-source, security-focused Linux distribution designed to provide network administrators, security auditors, and forensic analysts with a comprehensive arsenal of open-source network security and diagnostic applications. Developed since 2003 by Ronald W. Henderson and Paul Blankenbaker, NST transforms standard x86_64 computer hardware or virtual machines into enterprise-grade network monitoring and intrusion analysis appliances. Built on the Fedora Linux foundation, NST integrates hundreds of security utilities unified under a sophisticated, browser-based administrative console.
content.what_is_it: Technically, Network Security Toolkit is a bootable live distribution based on Fedora (NST 44 synchronizing with Fedora 44 and powered by modern Linux kernels). It packages more than 250 security and networking utilities, including Wireshark/TShark, ntopng with nDPI (Deep Packet Inspection), Snort, Suricata, softflowd, Nmap, and OpenVAS/GVM. The core distinguishing architectural feature of NST is the NST Web User Interface (NST WUI), an advanced web console accessible over HTTPS on port 9943 that automates packet capture, host geolocation mapping, bandwidth monitoring, and service auditing through an intuitive graphical dashboard.
content.origin_and_history: Ronald W. Henderson and Paul Blankenbaker founded the Network Security Toolkit project in 2003, initially assembling a compact bootable CD based on Red Hat Linux to facilitate on-site security diagnostics without installing software on client machines. Over more than two decades of continuous development, the toolkit migrated to Fedora as its upstream base and systematically incorporated the top security utilities cataloged by Insecure.org (now SecTools.Org). Major release milestones (such as NST 28, NST 34, NST 42, and NST 44 in June 2026) introduced deep packet inspection charts, automated IPv4/IPv6 entity discovery, Bluetooth BLE monitoring, and integration with modern containerized and virtualized server infrastructures.
content.governance_and_development: Network Security Toolkit is maintained as an independent open-source project led by its original co-founders. Code development, packaging recipes, and Subversion (SVN) source repositories are hosted publicly on SourceForge under the project identifier `nst`. The project maintains rigorous release schedules aligned with upstream Fedora milestones, publishing detailed package manifests (`manifest-44-15105.html`) and changelogs with every ISO release. Project funding relies on user contributions, consulting engagements, and community mirror bandwidth.
content.nst_wui_and_web_console_architecture:
The definitive operational component of NST is the NST WUI (Web User Interface). Accessible locally or remotely via encrypted HTTPS, the WUI eliminates the friction of configuring complex command-line syntax for multi-tier analysis workflows. Key features of the WUI include:

- Interactive Network Capture: Initiating multi-interface packet captures with tcpdump, TShark, and nDPI protocol classification, displaying live protocol distribution graphs.
- Host Geolocation: Mapping IP endpoints, autonomous system numbers (ASNs), and traceroute paths visually onto interactive global map overlays.
- Entity Extraction: Automatically discovering IPv4, IPv6, MAC, hostname, and Bluetooth addresses from shell console command outputs and piping them into diagnostic widgets.
- Bandwidth and Socket Monitoring: Real-time visual tracking of network interface bandwidth thresholds, coupled with socket-to-process inspection via `somo`.
content.deep_packet_inspection_and_netflow: For deep network visibility, NST integrates ntopng coupled with the nDPI (Deep Packet Inspection) engine. This framework identifies application-layer protocols even when encapsulated within non-standard ports or encrypted tunnels. In NST 44, the legacy ipt_netflow module was upgraded to `softflowd`, providing semi-stateful network flow monitoring that exports standardized NetFlow v5 and v9 records for post-capture traffic analysis and network accounting.
content.intrusion_detection_and_vulnerability_sc: NST bundles leading intrusion detection and vulnerability management suites. Network administrators can configure and monitor Snort and Suricata intrusion detection systems (IDS/IPS) directly from the WUI, correlating real-time attack signatures with system logs. Furthermore, NST integrates OpenVAS / Greenbone Vulnerability Management (GVM), enabling scheduled network vulnerability scans and regulatory security compliance audits across enterprise subnets.
content.desktop_environments_and_virtualization: For local graphical operation, NST deploys the lightweight MATE desktop environment, supplemented by minimalistic window managers (Fluxbox and Openbox) for resource-constrained systems. Beyond physical bare-metal deployments, NST is extensively optimized for enterprise virtualization. It can run as a virtual appliance under VMware ESXi, Proxmox VE, KVM, and VirtualBox, where virtual switches configured in promiscuous or port-mirroring mode allow NST to monitor all inter-VM network traffic across virtualized data centers.
content.installation_and_boot_capabilities: NST is distributed as a hybrid live ISO image compatible with legacy BIOS and UEFI firmware (including out-of-the-box support for UEFI Secure Boot via Fedora-signed bootloaders). It can be executed purely in RAM as an ephemeral live system, deployed to USB flash drives with LUKS-encrypted persistent storage via the `nstlive` utility, or permanently installed to physical hard drives and SSDs via an Anaconda-derived system installer to operate as a permanent security server.
content.threat_model_and_operational_limits:
Network Security Toolkit documents clear operational boundaries regarding its capabilities:

- Active Network Footprint: NST is an active diagnostic and penetration testing distribution; port scans, ARP sweeps, and packet injections emit detectable network traffic identifying the source IP address.
- No Automated Protection: NST does not function as an autonomous drop-in firewall that secures a network automatically; it requires human analytical expertise to configure rules and interpret diagnostic alerts.
- Absence of Tor Routing: NST does not route system traffic through the Tor anonymity network by default, making it unsuitable for undercover investigations without external proxy encapsulation.
content.privacy_and_telemetry: Network Security Toolkit enforces a strict non-commercial, zero-telemetry policy. The distribution contains no advertising frameworks, proprietary telemetry daemons, or background analytics phoning home to central servers. Package updates and repository interactions occur directly over standard HTTP/HTTPS connections through official Fedora and NST mirror repositories without transmitting user identifiers.
advantages: Sophisticated Web User Interface (NST WUI) managing over 250 top security and diagnostic tools through a web browser
Robust packet analysis and Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) integrating Wireshark, ntopng, nDPI, and softflowd NetFlow
Integrated intrusion detection suites (Snort, Suricata) and vulnerability scanning with OpenVAS/GVM
Interactive host geolocation mapping overlaying network hops and GeoIP data on geographical maps
Flexible deployment spanning live boot, LUKS-encrypted USB persistence, permanent disk installation, and virtual appliances
Stable foundation based on Fedora with out-of-the-box UEFI Secure Boot compatibility
Zero commercial telemetry policy with public SVN repositories and transparent package manifests
disadvantages: Steep learning curve requiring professional networking and packet analysis expertise to interpret diagnostic data
High memory consumption when running multiple heavy analysis daemons (ntopng, OpenVAS, Suricata) concurrently
Does not route network traffic through Tor by default, revealing the real source IP address during active audits
Web console listening on HTTPS port 9943 requires careful access control when exposed on shared subnets
Monolithic Linux kernel architecture lacking the bare-metal virtualization compartmentalization of Qubes OS
who_is_it_for: Network engineers, system administrators, and security operations center (SOC) analysts monitoring enterprise subnets
Security auditors and penetration testers performing protocol inspection, bandwidth analysis, and vulnerability scans
Infrastructure teams deploying dedicated virtual network monitoring appliances on VMware, Proxmox, or KVM hypervisors
Cybersecurity educators and students studying network protocol behaviors and packet-level forensic analysis
who_is_it_not_for: Whistleblowers and activists seeking an amnesic, anonymous web browsing system (better suited to Tails or Whonix)
Casual non-technical desktop users seeking a general everyday workstation operating system
Offensive red teamers requiring covert, low-footprint wireless exploitation platforms (better suited to Pentoo or Kali Linux)
